What changes from a prototype to a repeat batch?

A prototype helps you check the design before ordering more parts. For a repeat batch, use the approved drawing revision and confirm the material and finish. You also need an agreed inspection plan and delivery terms. The quantity that makes a small batch economical depends on the part and its setup, not a fixed industry threshold.

Prototype and repeat-batch planning compared
Decision	Prototype / first sample	Repeat or small batch
Drawing revision	Use the sample to identify fit, function or appearance questions.	Release one controlled revision for the quoted batch; agree how revisions are approved and changed features identified.
Setup & route	Review workholding and access while confirming the design.	Confirm the setup and sequence for the released revision, critical datums, and whether the route changes with quantity.
Material & finish	Check the specified grade, condition and final appearance.	Retain the approved specification unless changed by agreement; confirm material documents, finish standard, masking and dimensions after treatment.
Inspection	Define fit, function and sample acceptance checks.	Identify batch sampling and critical-feature records; confirm method, instrument evidence and report format available.
Price & timing	Confirm the prototype price and schedule for the specific part.	Requote the batch quantity and price; production takes 7–14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including finishing. Add transit separately.
AI-generated illustrative image. It is not an LZZ order, delivered quantity or production record.
What changes from a prototype to a repeat batch?

For a first sample, agree what must be learned or approved: assembly fit, a critical interface, operation or appearance. For a repeat order, carry the approved drawing revision, material and finish into the quotation, then agree the acceptance plan and the documents to accompany delivery. If the drawing changes after approval, pause and confirm the impact before treating the old sample as representative.

What are the minimum order and production lead time?

The minimum order is 1 piece. Production takes 7–14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including surface finishing. Shipping time is additional. Share the part, quantity and arrival date so LZZ can quote price and delivery arrangements.

How can I compare prototype suppliers?

Compare the quoted scope, not headline unit price alone. Check that each quote uses the same drawing revision, material and finish; that setup, inspection records, packaging and delivery basis are stated; and that any exclusions or substitutions are clear. Ask how changes, nonconforming parts and repeat orders will be handled.

Request a quote for the next batch

Share the drawing, first-order quantity, expected repeat pattern and required arrival date. Identify critical dimensions and records, then confirm price, production slot, inspection evidence, finish, packing and shipping terms for that order. The ordering guide explains the information to agree before shipment.

Finishing services and acceptance points

We support deburring, bead blasting, polishing, anodizing, passivation and plating as appropriate to the selected material. The quotation defines the finish and any accompanying documents; not every treatment is suitable for every alloy.

Deburring and polishing: specify edge breaks, cosmetic faces and any controlled roughness.
Bead blasting: agree appearance, protected interfaces and whether a reference sample is needed.
Anodizing: specify alloy, color, coating requirements and masked threads or mating surfaces.
Passivation and plating: identify the applicable material, process specification, protected areas and acceptance documents.

Critical dimensions are checked at the agreed stage, including after finishing where required. We link the material and treatment documents requested in the order to the relevant part or batch reference.

Describe the operating conditions

Explain the weight and loading requirements, along with the part's exposure and operating temperature. Describe its electrical behavior and the assembly it mates with. If you have not selected a grade, share these conditions and the applicable specification for engineering review. A catalog category does not establish suitability for a safety-critical application.

Specify the material grade

The catalog groups parts by material: aluminum, stainless steel, copper and brass, and engineering plastics. Each group covers different grades. State the grade and condition your design requires, then confirm whether alternatives are permitted and which material documents you need.

Material examples named in the original brochure
Aluminum: 6061, 7075 and 2024.
Stainless steel: 304, 316 and 17-4PH.
Copper and brass: printed as C3600 and H62 in the source brochure.
Engineering plastics: POM, PEEK and PPSU.
Other named materials: titanium, Inconel, Kovar and Invar.

This list preserves examples from the source brochure; it does not confirm current stock or availability. Confirm the exact alloy designation, grade, condition, process suitability and material documents for each part. In particular, verify the intended C3600 designation before quoting.

Compare material families by the job
Family	Examples in the brochure	Compare and confirm
Aluminum	6061, 7075, 2024	Compare strength/stiffness, part mass, environment and finish needs. Confirm exact alloy/temper, alternatives, finish compatibility and documents.
Stainless steel	304, 316, 17-4PH	Compare environment, mechanical requirements and condition. Confirm grade, heat treatment where applicable, finish, standard and certificates.
Copper / brass	C3600, H62 as printed	Compare electrical or thermal role and service environment. Confirm the alloy designation and material documents. Check the brochure's C3600 reference with us before ordering.
Engineering plastics	POM, PEEK, PPSU	Compare temperature, load, chemical exposure, electrical behavior and mating material. Confirm exact grade, operating conditions and traceability documents.

These are comparison prompts, not a material recommendation. Properties vary by grade, condition and design; confirm the requirements with the drawing and applicable specification.

How should I compare material options?

Compare named grades against the part's load, weight, temperature, environment, electrical or thermal function and mating components. “Aluminum,” “stainless” or “plastic” alone is not a purchase specification: grade, condition and applicable standard matter. Ask whether a substitute is acceptable and what material documents can accompany the order.

The image at the top is an AI-generated illustration of generic component forms, not a verified material sample; use a material specification or certificate when grade identification matters.

Define the finish requirements

Specify visual appearance separately from the finish's function. Name the required finish standard and revision where applicable, and describe color, gloss, texture, coating thickness or roughness only where these are controlled requirements. Mark masked areas, cosmetic faces and surfaces for corrosion protection, electrical contact or sealing. Confirm process suitability, availability and required documentation for the selected material and part.

A photograph shows surface appearance but cannot establish coating thickness or surface roughness. It cannot verify process compliance either, so a reference image alone is not a finish specification.

AI-generated illustration. The pictured finishes are not LZZ samples and do not identify a coating, roughness value or process standard.
Resolve dimensions after treatment

Tell the supplier whether acceptance dimensions apply before or after finishing. Highlight mating bores, threads and other interfaces where a coating matters. Specify edge breaks and cosmetic faces separately so functional and appearance criteria can be reviewed together.

Record the requirements in your RFQ

Put the agreed material and finish requirements on the controlled drawing or specification. Include inspection and traceability needs in your RFQ package, using the quality checklist to check the details before you prepare an inquiry.

site information

Information about inquiry drafts, browser storage and the product details on this site.

Your inquiry

The form creates an email draft in your browser. It does not send your information to LZZ or upload drawings. To contact us, open the draft in your email app, add your attachments and send it yourself.

Saved drafts

The form saves your input and draft status in the current tab using sessionStorage, with a separate entry for each selected part. Your details stay available after a refresh but are not saved to an account or sent to LZZ. Select "Clear saved input" to remove the entry for the current part.

Your browser may restore this data when it restores a previous session. Clear your input before leaving a shared device. If browser storage is blocked or full, you can still use the form while the page is open. Select "Save draft" to download a text copy.

Cookies and external services

This site does not use analytics or advertising cookies. Your email provider, WhatsApp and other linked websites have their own privacy policies.

Product and company information

Product pages show a catalog image; the image is not an inspection record or a specification document. Original workshop photographs and company documents are identified separately from product examples.

Product pages use shorter titles and summaries of the catalog entries. The original names remain available on those pages, and the source material is kept in our archive. The summaries are not independently verified specifications for the photographed parts. Confirm material grades and tolerances with the team, along with the inspection and commercial terms for your order.

The engineering guides help you prepare an inquiry; they are not inspection records or customer case studies. They do not establish suitability for a particular application. Material filters help you find existing parts without creating duplicate product pages. English descriptions of company documents explain their contents but do not verify current validity.

Contact

For questions, contact roger@lzz-cnc.com.

On this page

A prototype helps you check the design before ordering more parts. For a repeat batch, use the approved drawing revision and confirm the material and finish. What changes from a prototype to a repeat batch?

For a first sample, agree what must be learned or approved: assembly fit, a critical interface, operation or appearance. For a repeat order, carry the approved drawing revision, material and finish into the quotation, then agree the acceptance plan and the documents to accompany delivery. If the drawing changes after approval, pause and confirm the impact before treating the old sample as representative.

What are the minimum order and production lead time?

The minimum order is 1 piece. Production takes 7–14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including surface finishing. Shipping time is additional. Share the part, quantity and arrival date so LZZ can quote price and delivery arrangements.

How can I compare prototype suppliers?

Compare the quoted scope, not headline unit price alone. Check that each quote uses the same drawing revision, material and finish; that setup, inspection records, packaging and delivery basis are stated; and that any exclusions or substitutions are clear. Ask how changes, nonconforming parts and repeat orders will be handled.

Request a quote for the next batch

On this page
Finishing services and acceptance points

We support deburring, bead blasting, polishing, anodizing, passivation and plating as appropriate to the selected material. The quotation defines the finish and any accompanying documents; not every treatment is suitable for every alloy.

Deburring and polishing: specify edge breaks, cosmetic faces and any controlled roughness.
Bead blasting: agree appearance, protected interfaces and whether a reference sample is needed.
Anodizing: specify alloy, color, coating requirements and masked threads or mating surfaces.
Passivation and plating: identify the applicable material, process specification, protected areas and acceptance documents.

Critical dimensions are checked at the agreed stage, including after finishing where required. We link the material and treatment documents requested in the order to the relevant part or batch reference.

Describe the operating conditions

Explain the weight and loading requirements, along with the part's exposure and operating temperature. Describe its electrical behavior and the assembly it mates with. If you have not selected a grade, share these conditions and the applicable specification for engineering review. A catalog category does not establish suitability for a safety-critical application.

Specify the material grade

The catalog groups parts by material: aluminum, stainless steel, copper and brass, and engineering plastics. Each group covers different grades. State the grade and condition your design requires, then confirm whether alternatives are permitted and which material documents you need.

Other named materials: titanium, Inconel, Kovar and Invar.

How should I compare material options?

Compare named grades against the part's load, weight, temperature, environment, electrical or thermal function and mating components. “Aluminum,” “stainless” or “plastic” alone is not a purchase specification: grade, condition and applicable standard matter. Ask whether a substitute is acceptable and what material documents can accompany the order.

Define the finish requirements

Name the required finish standard and revision where applicable, and describe color, gloss, texture, coating thickness or roughness only where these are controlled requirements. Mark masked areas, cosmetic faces and surfaces for corrosion protection, electrical contact or sealing. Confirm process suitability, availability and required documentation for the selected material and part.
